title: Peripheral Pitting & Pain: PUK vs. Mooren’s Ulcer
summary: A comprehensive clinical breakdown of peripheral corneal melting syndromes. This poster distinguishes between Peripheral Ulcerative Keratitis (PUK)—a manifestation of systemic vasculitis—and Mooren’s Ulcer—a rare, idiopathic, sight-threatening autoimmune keratitis.

sections.title: Clinical Definitions
sections.content: Peripheral Ulcerative Keratitis (PUK) is a crescent-shaped destructive inflammation of the juxtalimbal corneal stroma associated with an epithelial defect, stromal thinning, and inflammatory cell infiltration. Mooren's Ulcer is a specific, idiopathic form of PUK that occurs in the absence of any detectable systemic autoimmune or infectious disease, characterized by an overhanging leading edge of deep stromal melting.

sections.title: The Great Comparison: PUK vs. Mooren’s

rows: Spares the limbus (usually starts near it)
Vessels grow into the ulcer base
Unilateral, older patients, slow progression, responds well to surgery/medical Rx.
Bilateral, younger patients (often African/Asian), rapid progression, poor prognosis.

sections.title: Pathophysiology: The Cascade of Melt
content: Step 1: Immune complex deposition (Type III Hypersensitivity) in the limbal vascular network.
Step 2: Recruitment of neutrophils and macrophages to the limbus.
Step 3: Release of Matrix Metalloproteinases (MMP-1, MMP-2, MMP-9) and Collagenases.
Step 4: Destruction of corneal stromal lamellae and epithelial basement membrane.
Step 5: Stromal melting proceeds circumferentially and then centrally.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup: Mandatory Labs
content: Complete Blood Count (CBC) with differential
ESR and C-Reactive Protein (CRP)
Rheumatoid Factor (RF) & Anti-CCP
ANCA (c-ANCA for GPA, p-ANCA for PAN/MPA)
ANA (Antinuclear Antibody) profile
BUN/Creatinine & Urinalysis (check for renal involvement)
Chest X-Ray or CT (rule out GPA/Sarcoid)
Syphilis Serology (RPR/FTA-ABS)

sections.title: The 'Red Flag' Symptoms
content: Extreme pain disproportionate to clinical findings (suggests Scleritis/GPA)
Sudden decrease in vision (threatened perforation)
Positive Seidel test over the area of thinning
Hematuria or hemoptysis (indicates systemic vasculitis emergency)
Scleral involvement (Sclerokeratitis indicates high systemic mortality risk)

sections.title: Management Algorithm
content: 1. Lubrication: Preservative-free tears and ointments.
2. Systemic Steroids: Oral Prednisolone (1mg/kg/day) for acute control.
3. Immunomodulators: Methotrexate, Azathioprine, or Mycophenolate.
4. Biologics: Rituximab (highly effective for GPA/refractory RA) or Infliximab.
5. Collagenase Inhibitors: Oral Doxycycline (100mg BID) and topical Medroxyprogesterone.

sections.title: Surgical Intervention Techniques
content: Conjunctival Resection: Removes the source of collagenases and antibodies (Primary for Mooren's).
Cyanoacrylate Tissue Adhesive: For small perforations (<1mm) or extreme thinning.
Amniotic Membrane Transplantation (AMT): Multilayered to promote epithelialization.
Tectonic Lamellar Keratoplasty: Crescentic grafts to restore globe integrity.
Gundersen Flap: If visual potential is poor but globe needs stabilization.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: PUK may be the presenting sign of a lethal systemic vasculitis (e.g., GPA).
A patient with RA who develops PUK has a 50% mortality rate at 10 years if not treated systemically.
Mooren's ulcer is a diagnosis of EXCLUSION. Always run the full vasculitis panel first.
Topical steroids can sometimes ACCELERATE melting in PUK by inhibiting collagen synthesis.

sections.title: Recent Advances: The Rituximab Revolution
sections.content: Landmark studies have shown that B-cell depletion therapy with Rituximab is superior to traditional cyclophosphamide for induction of remission in ANCA-associated vasculitis (RAVE and RITUXVAS trials). In PUK associated with Wegener's (GPA), Rituximab has become a first-line agent, showing rapid stabilization of the corneal stroma and better safety profiles than older alkylating agents.
